newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Feb 12.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Feb 12.

text.p: THE DOMINION

A drunken driver who killed four people will continue to get weekly ACC payments after the High Court at Wellington on Tuesday rejected a bid by ACC to stop paying the man. ACC had stopped paying the man, as a test case, arguing that, even though ACC was introduced as a no-fault system, it would be repugnant to justice to pay compensation to such a drunken driver. ACC Minister Jenny Shipley said on Tuesday night that the government would review the law because it was increasingly clear it did not meet public expectations. Page 1.

The government would not take "precipitate action" over the high exchange rate, Treasurer Winston Peters said on Tuesday. After a speech to business leaders in Wellington, Peters took a hands-off approach to the exchange rate. He said he would not react to a "perceived short-term crisis" with the exchange rate and would let the market respond as it saw fit. "The market itself is a clear commentator on what the exchange rate level should be," he said. Page 1.

NZ First leader Winston Peters on Tuesday criticised the "indulgences" of people at the embattled Aotearoa Television Network but stopped short of naming MP Tukoroirangi Morgan, who took part in a controversial spending spree. Morgan, who spent about $4000 of ATN money on clothes in September before he was elected to Parliament and after he had resigned as a director, also escaped the scrutiny of NZ First MPs at their caucus meeting on Tuesday. Page 1.

The government might appeal against the High Court's ruling that student loan money cannot be treated as income when declaring whether someone is eligible for benefits. Social Welfare Minister Roger Sowry said on Tuesday that only a small group of people -- "we're taking hundreds rather than anything larger" -- were affected by the ruling. Page 2.

Energy Minister Max Bradford on Tuesday called for supermarket chains to sell petrol to increase competition after citing evidence of importers' rising profit margins. The evidence was of "concern to the government", Bradford told an

energy sector conference in Wellington. Bradford's office later produced a Commerce Ministry graph showing that the difference in Singapore export prices and the New Zealand retail price of unleaded petrol had increased steadily since 1990 from 15 cents a litre to about 22.5c a litre in real terms by the third quarter of 1996. Page 20.

Difficult trading in pulp and liner board markets and flat export log prices have cost Carter Holt Harvey dearly with earnings down 56 percent to $171 milion for the nine months to December 31. Reaction to the slump was swift on Tuesday with
eight cents wiped off the share price to $3.25 by close of morning trade, and another one cent drop in the afternoon. Page 20.

The government was taken to task by business people on Tuesday for the impact of government charges, rules and regulations and compliance costs. At a government to business forum, Ngai Tahu Trust Board chairman Sir Tipene O'Regan questioned the government's competence to deliver cost-effective services to the fishing industry. There was a serious problem if the compliance regime was "almost utterly ineffective and
imposing inappropriate cost", Sir Tipene said. Such compliance costs were a serious disincentive to employment, he said. Page 20.

National Mutual Holdings said on Tuesday that trading for the first quarter of its current year suggest its profit for 1997 would exceed the A$210.9 million (NZ$234 million) reported in 1996. Chairman Athol Lapthorne told the company's annual meeting in Melbourne that the insurer and fund manager was well placed to meet the challenges in its market. Page 21.

Wang New Zealand said on Tuesday its interim profit's rise in the face of a fall in sales value indicated the move from hardware vendor to systems integration and services was going according to plan. Net profit for the first half to December 31 was up 10.8 percent to $1.72 million, whereas sales were down 10.8 percent to $33.93 million, Wang said. Page 21.

New Zealand investors will have the chance to make a leveraged investment in Telecom through a call warrant issue, the first such issue for many years. German commercial bank Deutsche Bank AG announced details on Tuesday of an issue of

call warrants over Telecom. Deutsche Bank will issue 50 million warrants with two warrants for each share exercised through brokers Garlick and Co. The warrants have an expiry date of September 23 next year and will have an exercise price of $3.80 for each warrant. Page 21.

Central banks should be cautious about responding to strong equity markets and growth because they might not trigger inflation in the same way they used to, according to a visiting United States analyst. Stephen Poloz, attending a FPG Research funds management conference this week, said many world

economies, such as the United States, were experiencing a supply shock -- effectively the opposite of the oil price shock in the 1970s. This was creating a bull equity market which was likely to continue in the long term. Page 22.

EMCO, the electricity market operating company, could scrap its day-ahead market after a review. Chief executive Lincoln Gould confirmed on Tuesday that axing the market was a possibility if market participants didn't use it. The day ahead market has been shunned since the wholesale electricity market began operating last October, participant preferring the
real-time market. Page 22.

Steel products manufacturer and distributor Steel and Tube Holdings posted a new profit for the five months to November 30 of $11 million, down three percent on the previous corresponding five months. The company said in a statement to the Stock Exchange that it expected to post a final 11-month result at the end of May which will approximate the previous period. Steel and Tube has changed its balance date to match Australian parent Broken Hill Proprietary. Page 22.

Macraes Mining Company has told the New Zealand and Australian stock exchanges it knew of no reason for the fluctuation in its share price last week. The Australian Stock Exchange had written to the company, saying it had noted the fluctuation in its share price from A$2.70 (NZ$3.02) on Monday last week to A$2.50 this Monday. Page 22.

CSI, a Britain-based distributor of television sports programming, has acquired a 50 percent stake in Auckland-based sports and leisure marketing consultancy James Dale Associates. James Dale, which employs ten permanent staff, is owned and
managed by Peter McDermott, immediate past chairman of New Zealand Cricket, and Roger Mortimer, a sports personnel management specialist. Page 22.

The government's decision not to boost the funding of Tradenz by $5 million would jeopardise a number of planned programmes to help exporters, the organisation's chairman, Gavin Cormack, said. Criticism of the government's business assistance package ignored the reality that exporting was, and would continue to be, a critical element of New Zealand's small economy, he said. Page 22.
